title: Hezekiah's Illness, Healing, and Fateful Hospitality
summary: Isaiah tells the gravely ill Hezekiah that he will die, but the king prays and weeps, and the LORD answers with fifteen more years and a promise to defend Jerusalem. As a sign, the shadow on the stairway of Ahaz goes back ten steps. When envoys come from the Babylonian king Merodach-baladan, Hezekiah shows them all his treasures, and Isaiah announces that everything will one day be carried off to Babylon, along with some of his descendants.
story: The deliverance from Sennacherib in chapter 19 is the high point of Hezekiah's reign, and this chapter closes it with two stories that pull in opposite directions. The first shows the LORD answering a king's tears with life. The second shows the same king, flattered by attention from a distant power, laying open his kingdom to strangers. The chapter quietly turns the book's attention from Assyria to Babylon. Assyria has just been humbled; Babylon, still a minor kingdom in rebellion against Assyria, is named for the first time as the power that will one day empty Jerusalem. Isaiah's words in verses 17-18 hang over every chapter that follows until they are fulfilled in chapters 24 and 25. The chapter then ends with Manasseh, who was only twelve when he became king (21:1) and so was probably born in those added years, and whose reign will be the worst in Judah's history.
historical:
The phrase "in those days" (verse 1) places these events loosely, and they are probably told out of order. The promise in verse 6 that the LORD will deliver Hezekiah and the city from Assyria suggests that the illness came before or during the crisis of 701 BC. Hezekiah reigned twenty-nine years (18:2), and fifteen added years fit an illness around 702 or 701 BC with his death around 686 BC.

Merodach-baladan (Marduk-apla-iddina in Babylonian sources) was a Chaldean leader who seized the throne of Babylon and held it against Assyria from about 721 to 710 BC, and then briefly again around 703 BC, before Sennacherib drove him out. His embassy to Hezekiah was almost certainly more than a get-well visit: he was looking for allies in the west against Assyria, which helps explain why Hezekiah showed off his treasury and armory. The tunnel of verse 20 is one of the best-known finds of biblical archaeology. Hezekiah's tunnel, cut through rock beneath the City of David to bring water from the Gihon spring to the pool of Siloam inside the walls, still exists, and an inscription found in it in 1880 describes the moment when the two crews digging from opposite ends met. Second Chronicles 32:30 also describes this work.
cultural:
Isaiah's instruction to put your house in order meant settling family and royal affairs, including the succession, before death. A poultice of figs was a recognized remedy for boils and skin infections in the ancient world, applied as a hot plaster. The text sets the medical remedy and the miraculous sign side by side without tension: God heals, and a remedy is used.

The stairway of Ahaz was apparently a set of steps on which the shadow of the sun moved as the day went on, working as a kind of timekeeper. Whether it was built for that purpose is not known. In the ancient Near East, displaying one's wealth to foreign envoys was a way of presenting oneself as a desirable ally, and sharing an inventory with a potential partner signaled trust. The word translated eunuchs in verse 18 was used for royal officials generally, but it often meant men who had been castrated to serve in the palace, and the prediction is severe: Hezekiah's line would serve a foreign court.
literary: The chapter has three scenes, each built on a dialogue between Hezekiah and Isaiah. In the first (verses 1-11), a word of death is reversed by prayer, and a sign confirms the reversal. In the second (verses 12-19), a word of judgment follows a proud display, and Hezekiah's response is left ambiguous. The two scenes are linked by the verb to see: the LORD has seen Hezekiah's tears (verse 5), and the Babylonians have seen everything in his palace (verse 15). The first seeing brings healing; the second will bring exile. Isaiah's questions in verses 14-15 are like a prosecutor's, and Hezekiah answers with a kind of naive pride. The regnal conclusion (verses 20-21) returns to the formula, mentioning the tunnel and naming Manasseh.

doctrines.note: The LORD's answer is explicit: I have heard your prayer; I have seen your tears. Hezekiah's prayer changes what happens, which shows that God invites his people into real conversation with him, not mere resignation.
The LORD adds years to Hezekiah's life and uses both a fig poultice and a miraculous sign. God's care works through ordinary means and extraordinary ones alike.

Isaiah's word about Babylon shows that Jerusalem's deliverance from Assyria was not a guarantee for all time. The city's future depended on its faithfulness, and the seeds of its fall were already present in its king's pride.

words.note: Rapha, to heal. The verb appears in the LORD's promise, I will surely heal you (verse 5), and in Hezekiah's request for a sign (verse 8). In Exodus 15:26 the LORD calls himself the LORD who heals. Here healing is personal, a response to a particular man's prayer and tears.

Ot, sign. A sign in the Old Testament is a visible event or object that confirms God's word, whether ordinary (like the rainbow) or miraculous. Hezekiah asks for one, unlike his father Ahaz, who refused a sign offered by Isaiah (Isaiah 7:10-12). The sign of the shadow confirms the promise of healing and deliverance.

Saris, eunuch or court official. The word can mean a high officer without implying castration (it is used of Potiphar in Genesis 39:1), but in a foreign palace it often did mean a castrated servant. The prediction of verse 18 is often connected with the Judean youths serving in the Babylonian court in Daniel 1, though the text of Kings does not name them.

christ: The link to Christ here is thematic. Hezekiah, a son of David, faces death, prays, and is told that on the third day he will go up to the house of the LORD. His reprieve is real but temporary: fifteen years later he dies, and his descendants are carried off to Babylon, as Isaiah warned. The New Testament proclaims a son of David who also prayed with tears to the one who could save him from death (Hebrews 5:7), who did die, and who rose on the third day never to die again. Hezekiah's story also exposes the limits of even the best king of Judah: he trusted the LORD greatly, yet his pride and short sight put his kingdom at risk. The book keeps waiting for a king whose faithfulness would not fail.

hard.q: Did God change his mind about Hezekiah's death, and was Hezekiah's response to Isaiah selfish?
hard.a:
Isaiah first says Hezekiah will not recover and then, after the king's prayer, brings a promise of fifteen more years. Some readers take this as God genuinely responding to prayer in a way that changes the outcome, as the Bible often describes. Others emphasize that God's announcements of judgment are often conditional, even when the condition isn't stated, as with Jonah's message to Nineveh; the warning was meant to lead to a response. Both views agree that prayer is not a formality and that God's purposes include the prayers of his people.

Hezekiah's words in verse 19 are debated too. Many readers find them self-centered: relieved that the disaster will come after his lifetime. Others read them as humble acceptance of God's word as just, with the thought of peace in his own days as an expression of relief that the judgment was deferred. The narrator gives both his spoken words and his private thought, and leaves the reader to weigh them.

questions: Hezekiah turned his face to the wall and wept, and God said, I have seen your tears. What does that suggest about how God receives honest grief?
Hezekiah showed the Babylonians everything he had. When are you tempted to seek the admiration of powerful people by displaying what you have?
Hezekiah seemed content that judgment would come after his lifetime. What responsibility do you carry for those who come after you?
